positions.text: Buterin and Griffith provide an independent cryptoeconomic qualification of Kaal’s validation-stage alignment mechanism. In Casper, validators post deposits, checkpoint-voting violations are objectively detectable, and evidence of either slashing-condition violation can be submitted on-chain to take the validator’s entire deposit. The paper further explains that the penalty can be set above the expected mining reward, making prohibited validation conduct economically unattractive. This supports the narrower mechanism that institutional validation can attach material cost to dishonest participation. Casper does not evaluate open-ended AI work, define low-quality outputs, or validate Kaal’s broader reputation substrate.

source_provenance.sourceProposition: Buterin and Griffith’s Casper makes validators’ deposits economically contingent on rule-compliant checkpoint voting: a detectable violation of either slashing condition can be submitted on-chain and causes loss of the entire deposit, with the penalty sized to exceed expected rewards.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Accountability. If a validator violates a rule, we can detect the violation and know which validator violated the rule. Accountability allows us to penalize malfeasant validators, solving the ‘nothing at stake’ problem that plagues chain-based PoS. The penalty for violating a rule is a validator’s entire deposit. This maximal penalty is the defense against violating the protocol. Because proof of stake security is based on the size of the penalty, which can be set to greatly exceed the gains from the mining reward, proof of stake provides strictly stronger security incentives than proof of work.
Each validator has a deposit; when a validator joins, its deposit is the number of deposited coins. After joining, each validator’s deposit rises and falls with rewards and penalties.

If a validator violates either slashing condition, the evidence of the violation can be included into the blockchain as a transaction, at which point the validator’s entire deposit is taken away with a small ‘finder’s fee’ given to the submitter of the evidence transaction.
